project.title: Sorting algorithms, measured
project.alt: Actual Sort Lab table comparing key comparisons and index swaps for three traces on the same custom input
project.desc: Compare sorting work on the same input, inspect each real trace and keep operation counts separate from measured runtimes.
project.built: Extended Sort Lab with complete operation comparisons and validated custom inputs while preserving all five Python implementations, their tests and traceable benchmark observations.
project.why: Two methods can produce the same answer while taking very different amounts of work. Correctness and measurement help make that trade-off visible.
how: Choose a generated pattern/size or enter 1–24 whole numbers; the same unchanged starting input feeds all three browser traces.
Compare complete key-comparison/index-swap totals, then open any trace, step backwards/forwards or reset to that exact input.
Inspect the separately measured five-algorithm Python benchmark, whose unchanged implementation/output hashes preserve the original observations.
project.demonstrates: Algorithmic reasoning, controlled comparisons, state management, regression testing and accessible interactive explanation.
project.caption: Genuine browser capture: complete trace totals for one shared custom input. These are key comparisons and index exchanges in JavaScript, not elapsed time or Python benchmark measurements.
project.result: Five Python implementations passed correctness checks on 125 measured sorts: five identical seeded random samples at each size from 50 to 1,000. Median and IQR are calculated from saved raw measurements. Measurements were recorded on Windows-11-10.0.26300-SP0 with Python 3.12.2; unchanged algorithm hashes reuse those observations. The browser explorer compares complete key-comparison/index-swap totals for three actual traces on the same generated or validated custom input. Selecting a trace and resetting preserve its starting values. These operation counts and animation pace are separate from the recorded Python runtime measurements.
project.limits: Measurements cover random non-negative integer inputs from 50 to 1,000 in one recorded environment; they do not establish a universal ranking. IQR describes observed variation, not confidence. Rightmost-pivot recursive quicksort has adverse-input recursion limits. Radix supports non-negative integers and rejects booleans/fractions. The browser explorer ports only three approaches and limits inputs to 24 values; animation pace is unrelated to Python runtime.
project.technical: Seven Python tests preserve algorithm correctness and benchmark-cache provenance. Five Node checks compare final traces with actual Python outputs, preserve every intermediate multiset, reconcile independently known counts and validate custom input syntax/bounds. Three browser journeys verify all row-to-trace totals, duplicate/custom input, retained-input resets, invalid-input recovery, playback and dense 24-value mobile layout. Cached traces make algorithm selection reuse the exact same input. Swaps count exchanges between different indices, including equal values; self placements are shown but not counted. Bar heights share a scale across each input and zero values remain visible. Python algorithm bytes and recorded benchmark data are unchanged.
project.run: Install requirements.txt; run python benchmark_portfolio.py, python plot_portfolio.py and python -m unittest discover -p "test_*.py" -v. Use --refresh to request new measurements. For browser verification, build Python fixtures and docs, npm ci, npm run test:trace and npm run test:browser.
gallery: The same custom values feed the selected trace, shared table and reset; small values use a readable common bar scale.
Preserved measured Python medians and observed IQR for five algorithms; playback pace never changes these measurements.
The same original benchmark observations at 1,000 values, on a linear scale.
project.demo_disclosure: Interactive browser explanation of three sorting approaches. Playback is illustrative; measured Python benchmarks are presented separately.
project.challenge: A comparison is only fair if every algorithm starts with the same values. The original controls regenerated input whenever the algorithm changed; deterministic examples hid that dependency. A shared current-input state and cached traces now keep custom values stable across selection, exploration and reset. Complete totals and in-progress counters are labelled separately, while the measured benchmark remains a separate experiment.
